reviews.text: Failed to really connect with the emotional side of this film at all. Didn’t think any of the performances were particularly great either and wasn’t a fan of the ending. Still held its own in other aspects but altogether it was just okay.

I was pretty disappointed with this one. I really love baseball, I love the rhythm of it, the empty moments, I love how the unique focus the sport has on the individual, while each one having to deal with the consequences or reaping the rewards of a teammates good at bat. I love the sound of the crack of a bat, the feeling of a ball in one's glove, its a really beautiful sport. The social aspects of watching it and the absolute marathon that a season is are all things I've grown to really appreciate. Sadly I don't really know what any of this has to do with this movie. This is a boy movie, a I feel smart boy movie all about one-upping people with math and being emotionally closed off and punching walls movie. It just all around really is not for me. The story of the Oakland A's at this time is neat, its cool that such an undervalued team was able to play the numbers and do well in a season. It's very cool that the style of get guys on base no matter how changed baseball strategies. I just didn't really gel with the performances or the way that this narrative was told. Brad Pitt really does not do it for me in this one, he's so closed off and shit eating grinning all the time it got pretty boring. I feel like Philip Seymour Hoffman is devastatingly under-utilized. Getting a man as talented as that in your film and having him just be a peeved coach with almost no screen time is an incredible let down. I cannot believe that Jonah Hill was the actor and character I enjoyed most, and got the most out of watching. His performance as a young kid in the industry who knows what he's saying but doesn't have the courage to speak it and relying on Billy to do so works very well! I am a huge huge fan of the use of real baseball footage, and the actors who play the players were cast tremendously and do a spectacular job making the transition to real footage completely seamless. The quiet moments where Billy is around the A's ballpark were when I really liked the film.

Prestige (derogatory). Operates very well on a whole bunch of levels with nothing too complex to actually say. Aaron Sorkin credit roll made a lot of things make sense retroactively (kept thinking Brad Pitt looked like him with that hair cut). Mostly the melodramatic temper tantrums and the childishly aggro and egoic social-verbal posturing. Engaging but not sustaining? That is to say the film has the bones to hang ideas from but pretty sparse meat and connective tissue. Also, there are no women in this movie who are people. Absolutely bored out of my gourd during all the trite family drama. Would have been stronger if the family had depth or their total one dimensionality was examined as it relates to the protagonist’s subjectivity. As it was, cloying and or unremarkable ciphers and cliches employed competently toward banally rank ends. On the subject of under utilized and developed characters, far too little Hoffman. I kept waiting for them to give him more to do and they never did. Overall idk. Looked great on film. Novel to see archival footage blended up with new stuff and used to tell the story. Lotta textural medium stuff I enjoyed. And of course how can you not be romantic about baseball?

• For some reason I didn’t like this movie when I saw it in high school, despite a topic that suited me extremely well. I decided to watch it again and my opinion definitely improved. • Brad Pitt delivers an excellent performance, bringing depth to a character that risked being one-dimensional. Jonah Hill is also impressive, but doesn’t quite do the same for his nerdy sidekick character. • There are many extended scenes or dramatic shots, often in slow-motion, and I feel this could have been cut to bring down the length of the movie. • The peripheral characters are all extremely resistant to the use of advanced metrics in baseball, it’s an exaggeration but works well for comedic effect, especially with the impeccable PSH as the bench manager.

Clearly not as high on this as others. I feel this movie is stuck in some sort if limbo with itself. It felt as if there were some plot points that they couldn’t decide whether or not they wanted to add so they decided to simply just pick and choose weird scenes to add and maybe keep some from entering the film. Like they really could have added more about his daughter, or could have just kept that part of the story altogether. And there was the one scene where he really starts developing good connections with the players, with essentially no payoff because they don’t win. It seems to be vaguely structured off a documentary so it makes sense that it feels jumpy at times but i just feel like im being forced to have my cake, but i can’t eat it. Sooo yeah eventually that cake goes bad. Also, if you told me going into this film my favorite performance after brad pitt would be chris pratt, i would have told you you’ve lost your mind, but here we are. I don’t like the pseudo-inspirational, pseudo-nostalgic score, especially when that is not what im taking away from the film. At the end of the day, it just was less than I expected. I can kind of lump it in with the social network by its subject matter, almost a historical retelling of something i don’t care much about. Perhaps it may be because I love baseball and everyone always tells me that I should love this movie. But this movie was hardly about baseball, it was trying to be about so many other things without committing to them. If it were moreso about jonah hill’s character, i would have been much more invested. Maybe i’m also just traumatized by how good he was at being an angry coach when he walked into jeremy giambi stripping on a table

"Sabermetrics" is the application of statistical analysis to baseball records, esp. in order to evaluate and compare the performance of individual players. The definition alone puts most people to sleep, and yet they made a movie about it. So if you haven't watch any of the trailers and don't know anything about it, Moneyball is the true story of Billy Beane (Brad Pitt), the manager of the Oakland A's who used the sabermetrics concept to stay within his ghetto Oakland budget in order to get a decent team. All the good players like Jason Giambi and Johnny Damon, after 2001, went on to play respectively for the Yankees and the Red Sox, the two most annoying and also wealthiest teams in the American league. In order to replace the star players, Billy Beane, with the help of Jonah Hill (who's character I don't know is fictional or not), crunched a bunch of numbers together to scout out the players that looked bad on paper, but because they statistically got on base a lot more, would be worth buying. This wasn't exactly a feel-good movie about how Beane used a revolutionary new method of scouting and brought a team to victory. Because, let's face it, does anyone remember Oakland winning a World Series any time since 1989? Hell no! Beane is still the GM of the A's and still, they suck big clanking moneyballs. But, the movie isn't about that. Aaron Sorkin, who co-wrote the screenplay, is a genius at getting a different message across. The Social Network wasn't about the invention of Facebook, it was about a nerdy guy who made a lot of complicated choices to become who he was. Moneyball is really about a guy who just tries a different philosophy. When Beane was in high school, the scouts all said he'd be a star player and convinced him to give up a Stanford scholarship to play for the Mets, but he bottomed out. As it's pointed out in Moneyball, this happens all the time. Not even just in baseball, but in most sports. Scouts really don't know jack shit about how a player is going to develop, so why not try this way? It seemed a perfect fit for Beane, who's portrayed by Pitt as a guy who wants badly to not have anything human to do with the players. He didn't want to have to get to know them, less he has to fire or trade them. He'd rather base everything on numbers, let the cold facts make the decisions for him. He struggles with it until he understand that you can't take romance about of baseball. These are human beings, not predictable machines, and Baseball is so ingrained in the American psyche as an escapist pastime that most people aren't going to easily accept something like sabermetrics. I liked Moneyball more than I thought I would. I didn't think there would be any point to basing a movie on something that didn't work. Hey, let's next do a movie on the development of New Coke! But, the theme sold me, and then so did Pitt's performance. Even Jonah Hill was good, not playing the sarcastic fat guy he's known for. I was hoping to see more of Oakland, but I mostly got scenes of that ghetto Coliseum, and all those shipyard structures, but that's just me. I shouldn't have expected Lake Merritt or something. The movie did last a long time so if you're not at all into baseball or the story, you might be looking at your watch.

Although baseball is at the heart of it, this is not a conventional sports drama that builds toward exaggerated highs and lows. Instead, it quietly follows the trajectory of one businessman’s passion. As someone who also has to confront the demands of work, I found parts of it deeply relatable, and I enjoyed the various moments that made me think, “Ah, I see.” Brad Pitt is very much Brad Pitt as the young executive who possesses both passion and ability, and there was something almost like an aesthetic ideal in the sheer perfection of his presence as that character.
